title: ERP invoice replication under storage and API pressure: 4-stage refactor

stages.scenario: An enterprise copies 50 million ERP invoice lines into custom objects with hourly ETL jobs. Data storage exceeds its allocation by 140%, and the jobs fail at peak hours when the daily API limit runs out, leaving reps with stale invoices. What is the root cause?

options.text: The invoice lines sit in standard storage when Big Objects would absorb the volume
options.coachingFeedback: Big Objects would relocate the copies but keep the hourly ETL, so the API exhaustion and stale invoices remain.

options.text: The hourly jobs use the REST API when Bulk API 2.0 would need far fewer calls
options.coachingFeedback: Bulk API would reduce calls, but the org would still store 50 million copied rows over its allocation, and reps would still see data as old as the last run.

options.text: Read-mostly reference data is replicated into transactional storage instead of queried at the source
options.coachingFeedback: Replicating high-volume, read-mostly data costs storage for every copied row and API calls for every sync, and the copy is only as fresh as its last run. All three symptoms trace to the copy itself.

stages.scenario: Reps need ERP invoices on Account pages, in reports, and in list views, current to the minute. Which pattern should replace the hourly copy?

options.text: A Lightning web component on Account that calls the ERP REST API through Apex
options.coachingFeedback: A custom component shows invoices on one page, but reports and list views cannot use data that exists only inside an Apex callout; request-reply is the suboptimal fit for this need.

options.text: Keep the ETL but narrow it to invoices from the last 90 days
options.coachingFeedback: A narrower copy reduces storage but keeps the hourly sync, so invoices stay up to an hour old and the jobs still compete for the daily API limit.

options.text: Salesforce Connect external objects, with an indirect lookup relating invoices to Account
options.coachingFeedback: External objects fetch ERP data live when a page or report uses them and store nothing in Salesforce. They work in page layouts, list views, and reports, and an indirect lookup relates them to Account through a unique External ID field.

stages.scenario: The external objects are built. Reps open invoices about 30,000 times a day, and the legacy custom objects hold the only Salesforce-side copy of the data. How should the team cut over?

options.text: Switch all users to external objects over a weekend after a full sandbox regression pass
options.coachingFeedback: A sandbox pass cannot reproduce production ERP load at 30,000 invoice views a day, and a single weekend switch leaves no tested fallback if the source struggles.

options.text: Pilot external objects with one team, then stop the ETL and purge legacy records in stages
options.coachingFeedback: A pilot checks source latency and lookup behavior under real use while the legacy copy still exists as a fallback. Only then should the ETL stop and the legacy records go in stages to reclaim storage.

options.text: Run external objects and the hourly ETL side by side so reps can use either
options.coachingFeedback: Running both keeps paying for the storage overage and API use the refactor exists to remove, and reps see two versions of each invoice with no exit point.

stages.scenario: After cutover, invoice views depend on the ERP's OData endpoint, which throttles above 50 requests per second and uses a credential that rotates every 90 days. What should the team monitor?

options.text: Salesforce data storage and daily API usage on the org's System Overview page
options.coachingFeedback: Those were the old ETL's failure signals; external object reads use neither Salesforce storage nor the daily API allocation, so both stay green while the ERP throttles.

options.text: An hourly synthetic query of one external invoice, alerting if it fails
options.coachingFeedback: An hourly probe catches a full outage, but not throttling at peak between probes or a credential about to expire.

options.text: OData callout latency, 429 and 500 responses, and upcoming credential expiry
options.coachingFeedback: Once reads depend on the ERP endpoint, its latency, throttling responses, and credential validity are what fail users. Event Monitoring's External OData Callout events expose callout timing, and an expiry alert catches the 90-day rotation first.
